extracted.intended_audience: mathematics educators, undergraduate instructors, and mathematics-education researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance (empirically grounded) on strategies students should use when reading mathematical proofs to improve comprehension; includes six named strategies illustrated with examples and survey evidence about mathematicians' preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the theorem statement (attend to assumptions and conclusions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before reading a proof, carefully understand the theorem statement, including its assumptions and conclusions, and how the claims in the proof relate to those assumptions and conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding the theorem statement enables comprehension of the meaning of claims in the proof and helps identify the proof framework that will be used to establish the theorem. The paper presents evidence (Study 1) that this strategy helped students understand proof structure and specific claims. In Study 2 survey items this general idea was presented in variants and generally received strong support from mathematicians. Instructional implication: emphasize parsing hypotheses and conclusions and mapping them to parts of the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Try to prove the theorem before reading its proof (variant A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempt to come up with your own proof or outline for the theorem before reading the given proof, using this as motivation and as a way to anticipate the proof framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits reported: provides motivation for reading the proof, helps anticipate the framework and structure used in the given proof, and primes the reader to notice key steps. Study 1 participants used this strategy; survey evidence indicated many mathematicians desire this behavior (Statement A in the survey). Pedagogical note: modeling and practice may be needed for students to apply this effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Try to prove the theorem before reading its proof (variant B — limited/contextspecific)
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative implementation of trying to prove first (used in Study 1 in at least one context) which some mathematicians view as not generally productive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study 2 results: majority of mathematicians (66%) preferred that students not use Strategy 1b; it was used only for one theorem/proof in Study 1 (Theorem 4/Proof 4) and may be beneficial only in particular contexts. Instructional caution: this variant should not be universally recommended without further evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the proof framework (attend to assumptions, conclusions, and technique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before or while reading line-by-line, identify the overall proof framework: what the main subclaims/propositions are, how assumptions are used, and what overarching technique or proof strategy is being employed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labeling propositions and mapping them to sub-proofs (e.g., naming assertions P and Q) helps clarify the role of assumptions and conclusions in each sub-proof. This strategy helps readers see why particular assumptions are appropriate and how the proof is structured. Study 2 survey evidence mostly supported this strategy, though about 23% of mathematicians favored a different ordering for engaging with new assertions (see paper).

rubrics_metrics.name: Break the proof into parts or sub-proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Partition long or complex proofs into smaller parts or sub-proofs that are individually manageable and can be summarized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits: makes complicated proofs tractable, enables summarization of structure, and helps the reader focus on the high-level claims rather than being mired in technical details. Example from Study 1: partitioning allowed students to focus on what each lemma/part established and how it supported the overall claim. Pedagogy: teach students to identify natural sub-proof boundaries and summarize each part.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use specific examples to make sense of confusing statements within the proof
rubrics_metrics.description: When an inference or line in a proof is confusing, instantiate the claim in a concrete example to see how the step applies and why it is valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study 1 vignette (n=24) shows two students using the specific number to (a) empirically verify the claim and (b) to understand why the chain of reasoning holds in general. Distinguish verification (adding up to check) from using the example to see the mechanism/reason that generalizes. This strategy is supported by prior maths-education literature and was favored by surveyed mathematicians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare the method in the proof to one's own methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflect on how the approach used in the proof differs from or resembles methods you would use; consider novelty and utility of the technique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparing approaches helps learners identify new techniques that might be useful in proving other results. Study 1 participants expressed that recognizing a clever or unfamiliar technique made the method an explicit object of discussion and helped them internalize it. Instructional implication: encourage students to note whether they'd have approached the problem similarly and to articulate why the presented method is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use social interaction (pair/group discussion) to facilitate strategy use
rubrics_metrics.description: Engage in dialog with peers (pairs or small groups) when reading proofs to externalize reasoning, ask clarifying questions, and adopt productive strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study 1 suggests working in pairs may facilitate the use of the above strategies (e.g., naming propositions to aid interaction, jointly marveling at techniques). Social interaction can help students internalize the dialogic forms of reasoning and adopt strategies. Pedagogical note: structured collaborative activities may increase uptake of proof-reading strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveats and limits (evidence strength and instructional challenges)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize limitations of the study's claims: small qualitative sample, limited number of proofs/domains, and historical difficulty of teaching heuristics effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper cautions that the strategies are an initial list rather than a comprehensive taxonomy. Prior efforts to teach problem-solving heuristics (e.g., Pólya-style) were often unsuccessful without substantial instructional design: content knowledge, beliefs, and prescriptive implementation details matter. The authors call for further research and design-based instructional interventions to evaluate how to teach these strategies effectively.
